title: Implement heap sort using a binary heap, explain the heapify and sort-down phases, and analyse its complexity and stability.

s1_definition.profdef: Heap sort is a comparison-based sort that first arranges the array into a binary max-heap, where each parent is at least as large as its children, then repeatedly swaps the maximum at the root to the end of the array and restores the heap over the shrinking front. It sorts in place with constant extra space and runs in n log n time in all cases, but it is not stable and has poorer cache behaviour than quick sort.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India arranges transaction amounts into a tournament bracket where every manager holds an amount at least as big as the two people reporting to them, so the biggest amount sits at the very top. A clerk takes the top amount, which is the largest, and places it at the end of the final sorted list, then promotes the right remaining amount back to the top by letting it sink to its proper level. She repeats: pull the current largest off the top, park it just before the previously parked ones, and re-settle the bracket. Each round extracts the next largest, so the list fills from the back with descending picks, ending up sorted.
s1_definition.oneliner: Build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root maximum to the end and sift down over the shrinking heap.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Heap sort is a comparison-based sort that first arranges the array into a binary max-heap, where each parent is at least as large as its children, then repeatedly swaps the maximum at the root to the end of the array and restores the heap over the shrinking front. It sorts in place with constant extra space and runs in n log n time in all cases, but it is not stable and has poorer cache behaviour than quick sort.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India arranges transaction amounts into a tournament bracket where every manager holds an amount at least as big as the two people reporting to them, so the biggest amount sits at the very top. A clerk takes the top amount, which is the largest, and places it at the end of the final sorted list, then promotes the right remaining amount back to the top by letting it sink to its proper level. She repeats: pull the current largest off the top, park it just before the previously parked ones, and re-settle the bracket. Each round extracts the next largest, so the list fills from the back with descending picks, ending up sorted.

**One line to remember:** Build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root maximum to the end and sift down over the shrinking heap.

sections.s2_technical:
Heap sort rests on representing a binary heap inside the array with no pointers: for an element at index i, its children are at two-i-plus-one and two-i-plus-two, and its parent is at i-minus-one over two. A max-heap satisfies the property that every parent is greater than or equal to its children, which forces the overall maximum to sit at index zero, the root.

The algorithm has two phases. First, build-heap turns the unordered array into a max-heap. The efficient way is to sift down every non-leaf node starting from the last parent and moving toward the root, which is O(n) overall, a non-obvious but important fact. Sift-down takes a node that may violate the heap property, compares it to its larger child, and swaps it down repeatedly until it is at least as large as both children. Second, the sort-down phase repeatedly swaps the root, the current maximum, with the last element of the active heap, shrinks the heap by one, and sifts the new root down to restore the heap. Each extraction places one element in its final sorted position at the back.

Because the array has n elements and each sift-down is log n, the sort-down phase is n log n, and this holds in every case, so heap sort has no quadratic worst case, unlike quick sort. It sorts entirely in place, needing only a constant amount of extra space, which is its advantage over merge sort. The sift-down procedure is the one piece of logic to get exactly right, including the bounds check so children indices do not exceed the active heap size.

A senior-level nuance is the trade-offs that keep heap sort out of the default spot despite its guarantees. It is not stable, because swapping distant elements reorders equal keys, and its memory-access pattern jumps around the array following parent-child indices, which is cache-unfriendly and makes it slower in practice than quick sort's sequential scans. Its real strength is the guaranteed n log n with constant space, which makes it valuable for memory-constrained or worst-case-sensitive settings, and the same heap structure, used as a priority queue rather than a full sort, is where heaps most often appear in production.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a sort on a memory-constrained processing node that forbids the linear extra buffer merge sort needs, yet also cannot tolerate quick sort's quadratic worst case on adversarial input. Heap sort uniquely gives in-place sorting with a guaranteed n log n bound.

Problem 2 — The node processes amounts into ascending order, and the sort must complete within a hard time budget regardless of input order, which heap sort's always-n-log-n behaviour satisfies.

In our mini-project we build an `InPlaceAmountSorter` that sorts an integer array ascending with heap sort, building a max-heap then extracting maxima to the back. The demo sorts an array and logs the result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the amounts fifty thousand, one thousand two hundred, ninety eight thousand, three hundred, seven thousand five hundred, twenty five thousand, four hundred.

Step 1: Build the max-heap. Starting from the last parent and moving toward the root, each node sifts down, swapping with its larger child until the heap property holds. After this phase the largest amount, ninety eight thousand, sits at the root at index zero.

Step 2: Begin the sort-down. Swap the root ninety eight thousand with the last element of the active heap, placing ninety eight thousand in its final position at the very end of the array.

Step 3: Shrink the active heap to exclude that final slot, then sift the new root down so the heap property is restored over the remaining elements. The next largest, fifty thousand, bubbles to the root.

Step 4: Swap the root fifty thousand with the new last active slot, parking it just before ninety eight thousand, then shrink and sift down again. The root now holds the next largest.

Step 5: Repeat the swap-shrink-sift cycle. Each round extracts the current maximum to the front of the sorted tail, so the array fills from the back with descending picks, which produces ascending order overall.

Step 6: When the active heap shrinks to one element, everything is placed. The array is sorted ascending, three hundred, four hundred, one thousand two hundred, seven thousand five hundred, twenty five thousand, fifty thousand, ninety eight thousand, achieved entirely in place with only a few temporary variables.

```
[2026-10-26 23:42:01] INFO    Sorted amounts: [300, 400, 1200, 7500, 25000, 50000, 98000]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  array as heap: child(i)=2i+1, 2i+2 ; parent=(i-1)/2

  Phase1 build max-heap (sift down last parent → root)
     root = 98000 (global max)

  Phase2 sort down:
     swap root↔last → park max at end; shrink; siftDown(root)
     [.....|98000]
     [....|50000 98000]
     [...|25000 50000 98000]  ... fills from back descending
  → ascending array, in place, O(n log n) all cases, NOT stable
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Heap sort is a comparison-based, in-place sort built on a binary heap represented directly inside the array, where for an element at index i the children are at two-i-plus-one and two-i-plus-two. It has two phases. First it rearranges the array into a max-heap, where every parent is at least as large as its children, which forces the overall maximum to the root at index zero. Then it repeatedly swaps that root maximum to the end of the active heap, shrinks the heap by one, and sifts the new root down to restore the heap property, so each extraction places one element in its final sorted position at the back.

The one piece of logic to get exactly right is sift-down: it takes a node that may violate the heap property, compares it against its larger child, and swaps it down repeatedly until it is at least as large as both children, with a careful bounds check so child indices do not exceed the active heap size. Building the heap by sifting down every non-leaf from the last parent toward the root is O(n), and the extraction phase is n log n, and that n log n holds in the best, average, and worst case, so heap sort has no quadratic blow-up. It sorts entirely in place, needing only constant extra space.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used heap sort on a memory-constrained processing node that could not spare the linear buffer merge sort needs, yet also could not risk quick sort's quadratic worst case on adversarial input and had a hard time budget. Heap sort uniquely gave me in-place sorting with a guaranteed n log n bound in every case, which is exactly that niche.

The senior-level point I make is why heap sort is rarely the default despite its guarantees. It is not stable, because swapping distant elements reorders equal keys, and its access pattern jumps around the array following parent-child indices, which is cache-unfriendly and makes it slower in practice than quick sort's sequential scans. So I reach for it specifically when I need in-place plus worst-case n log n, and I note that the heap structure itself is far more commonly used as a priority queue than as a full sort, which is where heaps really earn their keep in production.
